newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends in contango amid ample supply.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends in contango amid ample supply.

text.p: NYMEX crude prices ended Monday in contango for the first time in almost two years, as prices cratered under a flood of imports from Europe and West Africa, traders said.

"This all has to do with a lot imports coming over, from Europe, where there are a lot of refiners in maintenance . . . and poor market margins," said Al Lindseth, a trader with GSC Energy in Atlanta. He also noted imports from Nigeria.
April crude settled 79 cents a barrel lower at $20.49. April gasoline finished off 1.31 cents a gallon at 64.36 cents April heating oil ended off 1.00 cent at 53.08 cents a gallon.
The last time crude ended in contango was for the brief period of its contract expiry in May 1995.

Traders and analysts said they could not predict exactly how long the carry will last or how wide it will end up being, but they said fortunes of the oil complex generally were hitched to gasoline's ability to follow through on its traditional spring rally.
Gasoline typically rallys in the spring in anticipation of the summer driving season when gasoline demand peaks.
"One thing I am willing to say is that the (gasoline) crack will stay wide," said Lindseth.
The April gasoline-to-crude crack spread ended at $6.54 a barrel, it's highest level in more than a year, and rising from $6.30 Friday.
"There has been a lot of crack spead buying in the past week despite weakness in the outright," said a New York gasoline dealer.
The rich crack spread, an indication of refiner profitablity, should provide strong incentive for refiners to increase crude runs to produce gasoline - a supportive scenario for crude prices.

But, there still may be more crude supply than refiners can absorb short-term, traders said. They said the gasoline crack could remain strong, reflecting a rise gasoline demand, while the outright price rise could be restrained by continuing ample crude supply.

In its oil inventory report last Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute (API) said as of February 28, implied demand for gasoline was a seasonally high 7.9 million barrels a day. Crude stocks, however, were 5.2 million barrels above year ago.
Traders said the API report this week could follow the same pattern.
"We could see the increased crude imports show up in this report," said GSC's Lindseth said.

Crude prices have suffered in the past month as heavy winter refinery maintenance cut crude usage, allowing crude to stockpile. The already sated U.S. market now needs to aborb an increase in imports which were triggered by a weak cash market abroad creating a surplus of foreign crude, traders said.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
